reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods
chapter_title: Techniques for Maintaining Stable Drilled Shaft Excavations

sections.title: Naturally Stable Conditions
sections.body: Stable excavation conditions exist in dry soil, strong cohesive or cemented soils, and intact rock. Stability depends on hole diameter and depth, surface loads, construction vibrations, and time hole must remain open. Local experience provides guidance but does not eliminate need for site-specific information. Mixed conditions are common — cohesive overburden may allow dry open-hole drilling while underlying sands require additional support. Water-bearing sand below clay overburden can cause flowing sands or bottom heave if groundwater level exceeds base of excavation. Rock with low permeability (shale, chalk, massive rock) may permit dry excavation even below groundwater. Add water to hole during excavation of permeable rock (porous limestone, sandstone) rather than allowing inflow that brings fines or causes sloughing.
key_points: Naturally stable: dry soil, strong cohesive/cemented soils, intact rock
Mixed conditions common — separate methods may be used for different strata
Cohesive soils into water-bearing sand: risk of flowing sands or bottom heave
Add water to permeable rock holes rather than allowing inflow with fines

sections.title: Temporary Casing
sections.body: Temporary (tool) casing stabilizes excavation and is removed during or after concrete placement. Fluid concrete pressure provides borehole stability after casing removal. With engineer approval, temporary casing may be left in place when soils prone to squeezing or bulging if casing removed. Casing must be cleaned after each use — rough interior causes drag on concrete during extraction, necking/voids, cage displacement, or stuck casing. ADSC standard: outside diameter in 6-inch increments, 18 to 120 in. Segmental casing: metric sizes (1.2 m ≈ 47.25 in. for 48 in.; 3 m ≈ 118 in. for 10 ft) — design should include flexibility on sizes to allow cost-effective segmental casing. If casing size not specified, contractor typically uses O.D. 6 inches larger than specified shaft diameter to allow passage of full-diameter drilling tool below casing. Minimum wall thickness: typically ≥0.325 in.; >48 in. O.D. tend to have greater wall thickness; vibratory/impact installation may require greater thickness. Three installation methods: casing seated through drilled hole; vibro-driven ahead of excavation; twisted (oscillator/rotator) ahead of excavation. Vibratory casing installation: vibratory hammer causes temporary liquefaction of adjacent soil zone; most effective in sandy soils with shallow groundwater; casing into underlying rock difficult or impossible with vibratory method. Caution: vibratory installation causes vibrations that can affect nearby structures or cause settlement in loose sands; monitor vibrations during technique shaft installations; typically small at 50-70 ft but may extend further in hard/cemented layers. Telescoping casing process: progressively smaller diameter casings through multiple strata; economic advantage (smaller crane); O.D. of lower casing ≥6 in. smaller than casing above; most used for rock-bearing shafts with no skin friction considered in cased zone. Possible effects on axial resistance: casing through soil may alter stress conditions affecting side resistance; consider in design when temporary casing passes through design-contributing strata.
key_points: Casing must be clean after each use — rough surface causes concrete drag and cage displacement
ADSC standard: OD in 6-inch increments, 18-120 in.; segmental casing in metric sizes
Contractor typically uses casing OD 6 in. larger than specified shaft diameter
Vibratory installation: effective in sandy soils; may cause vibrations affecting nearby structures
Monitor vibrations during technique shaft; typically small at 50-70 ft distance
Telescoping casing: progressively smaller casings; most used for rock-bearing shafts

sections.title: Permanent Casing
sections.body: Permanent casing left in place as a form or structural element. Required when drilled shaft extends through open water or extremely soft/unstable soil layers. Types: standard steel pipe (OD standard sizes); corrugated sheet metal; special structural pipe. Permanent casing installed similarly to temporary casing using vibratory hammer, oscillator/rotator, or through pre-drilled hole. Effects on axial and lateral resistance: permanent casing eliminates side resistance in cased zone; must account for casing in structural design for lateral loading; corrosion of casing over design life must be assessed. Permanent casing through soft cohesive soils prone to squeezing helps prevent necking that could occur if temporary casing were removed.
key_points: Required for shafts through open water or extremely soft/unstable soil layers
Permanent casing eliminates side resistance in the cased zone — must account in design
Assess casing corrosion over design life for structural integrity
Prevents necking in soft soils prone to squeezing during casing extraction
sections.applicability: Marine construction; soft soil environments; structural design of cased zones

sections.title: Construction Using Drilling Fluids
sections.body: Drilling fluids maintain excavation stability by providing head pressure exceeding external groundwater pressure. Required in cohesionless soils below water table, in soft or unstable soils, or when excavation cannot be stabilized by casing alone. Types: (1) Water — used alone in stable but permeable rock formations or when minor seepage occurs; maintain head sufficient to prevent infiltration; (2) Bentonite slurry (mineral) — montmorillonite clay in water; increases viscosity and unit weight; forms filter cake at borehole wall reducing permeability; filter cake controls fluid loss but may reduce concrete/soil bond; density typically 8.5-9.0 lb/gal; (3) Polymer slurry (synthetic) — long-chain hydrocarbon molecules; increases viscosity without filter cake; greater fluid loss tendency than bentonite in coarse-grained soils; less effective in supporting coarse-grained soils or non-circular excavations; no filter cake = better side resistance performance; predominant method in North America; (4) Mineral/polymer blends — combine properties of both types. Fluid quality requirements before concrete placement: Bentonite — Marsh Funnel viscosity 28-40 sec/qt, density ≤1.15 g/cm³, pH 7.5-11, sand content ≤4%; Polymer — Marsh Funnel viscosity 34-80 sec/qt, density ≤1.01 g/cm³, pH 7-12, sand content ≤1%. Minimum positive head: slurry level ≥5 ft above piezometric surface for stability through granular soils. Effects on axial resistance: bentonite filter cake buildup on borehole wall can significantly reduce unit side resistance; polymer fluids show little or no reduction in side resistance when specification requirements are met; wet construction with properly managed fluids (bentonite or polymer) can produce resistance comparable to dry construction when fluid quality is maintained.
key_points: Minimum slurry head: ≥5 ft above piezometric surface; 10+ ft may be needed
Bentonite density: typically 8.5-9.0 lb/gal; forms filter cake — may reduce side resistance
Polymer: no filter cake = better side resistance; greater fluid loss in coarse-grained soils
Polymer predominant method in North America
Fluid quality before concrete: bentonite — Marsh Funnel 28-40 sec, density ≤1.15 g/cm³; polymer — 34-80 sec, density ≤1.01 g/cm³
Sand content: bentonite ≤4%; polymer ≤1%
Filter cake from bentonite can significantly reduce unit side resistance if not managed

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter described techniques for maintaining stable drilled shaft excavations: naturally stable conditions (dry, cohesive, intact rock); temporary casing (tool casing); permanent casing; and drilling fluids (water, bentonite, polymer, blended). Excavation stability must be maintained from start of drilling through completion of concrete placement and casing extraction. Contractor chooses appropriate method; designer must understand implications of each method for shaft performance and design.
